# Faster Algorithms for Finding Small Induced Patterns in Sparse Host Graphs

**Abstract.** We study algorithms to detect induced _G_-subgraphs, for fixed patterns _G_, given host graphs with _n_ vertices and _m_ edges as input. We show that:

- There are at least five 5-vertex connected graphs _G_ (out of 21) that can be detected in \(\widetilde{O}(nm)\)-time.

- There are at least sixty-five 6-vertex connected graphs _G_ (out of 112) that can be detected in \(\widetilde{O}(m^2)\)-time.

- The graphs _P_<sub>7</sub> and _C_<sub>7</sub> can be detected in \(\widetilde{O}(nm^2)\)-time.

Our main technical tool is a generalized notion of width of tree decompositions that we call (_p,q_)-width tree decompositions. We use (_p,q_)-width tree decompositions to derive algorithms with running-time \(\widetilde{O}(n^pmq)\) for detecting induced subgraphs. Our upper-bounds are never worse than existing upper-bounds and are faster when _m=o(n_<sup>2</sup>). Moreover, for some patterns, such as _C_<sub>7</sub>, our algorithms are optimal under standard complexity theoretic assumptions.

The new technique we use to obtain fast algorithms for fixed pattern graphs is not scalable to families of pattern graphs. We further refine this idea by constructing pattern-based polynomials that exploit the structure of the tree decomposition, and not just its width, to obtain algorithms for larger classes of graphs. We show:

- An \(\widetilde{O}(m^{k-1})\)-time algorithm for detecting induced _P_<sub>2_k_</sub> in bipartite graphs.

- An \(\widetilde{O}(nm^{k-1})\)-time algorithm for detecting induced _C_<sub>2_k_</sub> in bipartite graphs.

These algorithms improve the best known upper-bounds for general graphs.

**Keywords: Combinatorial Graph Algorithms** \(\cdot\) Induced Subgraph Detection \(\cdot\) Graph Pattern Polynomials.

### 1 Introduction

We consider the computational problem of finding induced copies of fixed _k_- vertex pattern graphs _G_ in a host graph _G_ with _n_ vertices and _m_ edges given as input. The straight-forward search algorithm for this problem takes _O(n<sup>k</sup>_)- time, which is polynomial-time since we regard _k_ as a constant. Williams [11] showed that even minor improvements to this trivial upper-bound can be used<tbc>

<tbc>to speed-up algorithms for NP-complete problems such as MAX2CNFSAT. In particular, they showed that the \(O(n^\omega)\)-time algorithm for triangle finding can be used to derive a \(O(2^{\omega n/3})\)-time algorithm for MAX2CNFSAT.

In a seminal paper, Nešetřil and Poljak [9] showed that every 3_k_-vertex pattern graph can be found in \(O(n^{\omega k})\)-time and asked the question whether there are patterns where we can do significantly better. To the best of our knowledge, there is only one pattern family for which we know a (slightly) better upper-bound than the one given by Nešetřil and Poljak [9]’s 41-year-old algorithm. Therefore, research on finding induced copies of fixed size patterns has focused on (1) improvements for small fixed patterns, mostly on four to nine vertices and (2) combinatorial algorithms, where we improve upon the trivial _O(n<sup>k</sup>_)-time bound without using fast matrix multiplication algorithms (See [1,5,10]). For example, Bläser, Komarath, and Sreenivasaiah [1] showed that there is a _O(n_<sup>5</sup>)-time algorithm for finding _C_<sub>7</sub> and recently Dalirrooyfard and Williams [3] showed that this is optimal assuming _K_<sub>5</sub> <sup>1</sup> requires _O(n_<sup>5</sup>)-time for combinatorial algorithms.

In practice, many host graphs in which we wish to find patterns are sparse. Therefore, there has also been research on deriving faster algorithms taking sparse host graphs as input. A common restriction is to assume that the host graph is _d_-degenerate for some fixed _d_ [2]. For example, we can find _C_<sub>7</sub> in _O(n_<sup>2</sup>)- time in a given _n_-vertex, _d_-degenerate graph. The _O(._) here hides factors that are exponential in _d_. Since the degeneracy of a graph can be as high as _n_, these algorithms are not suitable for arbitrary host graphs.

Another line of research to improve the running-time on sparse host graphs is to consider the running-time as a function on both the number of vertices and the number of edges in the host graph. For example, recently, Komarath, Kumar, Mishra and Sethia, [7] have shown that _C_<sub>6</sub> has \(\widetilde{O}(m^2)\)-time <sup>2</sup> algorithms. They obtained this improvement by defining matched treewidth, a new notion of width of tree decompositions. A key sub-routine in their paper is an algorithm to construct small _arithmetic circuits_ (Definition 7) for _graph homomorphism polynomials_ (Definition 10) when the pattern graph has small matched treewidth. To use these arithmetic circuits to find induced patterns, they then construct specific tree decompositions with the required matched treewidth and an additional property that the tree decomposition can be used to avoid duplicate homomorphisms to the same occurence of the pattern as a subgraph while constructing the circuit. However, their work is mainly about counting (not necessarily induced) subgraphs.

## Our results:

In this paper, we define a new notion of width for tree decompositions called (_p,q_)-width. The key ingredient behind our improved algorithms is a \(\widetilde{O}(n^pm^q)\)-time algorithm to construct arithmetic circuits for graph homomorphism polynomials from pattern graphs of (_p,q_)-width. Then, we construct specific tree decompositions with certain additional conditions that we call _au_

<sup>1</sup> The clique on five vertices <sup>2</sup> We use \(\widetilde{O}(.)\) to denote that we ignore factors logarithmic in the input size.

- There are at least five 5-vertex connected graphs _G_ (out of 21) that can be detected in \(\widetilde{O}(nm)\)-time.<tbc>

- There are at least sixty-five 6-vertex connected graphs _G_ (out of 112) that can be detected in \(\widetilde{O}(m^2)\)-time.<tbc>

**-** The graphs _P_<sub>7</sub> and _C_<sub>7</sub> can be detected in \(\widetilde{O}(nm^2)\)-time.

We derive _O(nm_), _O(m_<sup>2</sup>), and _O(nm_<sup>2</sup>) algorithms for detecting induced _P_<sub>5</sub>, _P_<sub>6</sub>, and _P_<sub>7</sub> respectively. To the best of our knowledge, the previous best algorithmic upper bounds which are given by Hoàng, Kaminski, Sawada, and Sritharan \[6\] for detecting induced _P_<sub>5</sub>, _P_<sub>6</sub>, and _P_<sub>7</sub> are _O(m_<sup>2</sup>), _O(nm_<sup>2</sup>), and _O(m_<sup>3</sup>) respectively when considering both number of vertices and edges of the host graph. Therefore, the above results improve existing bounds for lengths 5, 6, and 7 for the cases where \(m=\Theta(n^{1+\epsilon})\), \(0\le\epsilon<1\).

We give a \(\widetilde{O}(nm)\)-time algorithm for _C_<sub>5</sub> which is optimal. This algorithm is an improvement on the _O(n_<sup>3</sup>)-time algorithm given by Komarath, Kumar, Mishra, and Setthia \[7\] when _m=o(n_<sup>2</sup>). We stress that simply having a (1,1)-width tree decomposition for a pattern is not sufficient to derive a faster algorithm for finding induced copies. For example, the complete bipartite graph _K_<sub>2,3</sub> has a (1,1)-width tree decomposition. But, we could not derive \(\widetilde{O}(nm)\)-time algorithms for finding it as those tree decompositions do not have automorphism avoiding conditions. Our techniques for finding induced subgraphs are illustrated using an example in Section A.

One drawback of our method (and many existing methods such as the ones in \[1,5,10\] used to derive faster algorithms for finding induced patterns) is that the analysis of specific subgraphs do not scale to larger patterns. For example, our algorithm for _C_<sub>7</sub> requires constructing specific tree decompositions for over 100 graphs. Therefore, we do not believe it will be possible to extend our analysis, or similar approaches, to derive algorithms for _C<sub>k</sub>_ for arbitrary _k_. However, we show that by imposing natural restrictions on the host graph, for example, restricting them to bipartite graphs, the required analysis may become simple enough for infinite size pattern families. We show:

- An \(\widetilde{O}(m^{k-1})\)-time algorithm for detecting induced _P_<sub>2_k_</sub> in bipartite graphs.<tbc>

**-** An \(\widetilde{O}(nm^{k-1})\)-time algorithm for detecting induced _C_<sub>2_k_</sub> in bipartite graphs.

To the best of our knowledge, for general host graphs, the fastest algorithms to find induced _P_<sub>2_k_</sub> runs in time _O(n_<sup>2_k_-2</sup>) \[1\]. Note that our algorithm is never worse than this and is significantly faster when _m=o(n_<sup>2</sup>), with the catch that ours only work when the host graph is bipartite. Similarly, our algorithm for _C_<sub>2_k_</sub> improves upon the trivial _O(m<sup>k</sup>_)-time algorithm when \(m=\omega(n)\).

Observe that an \(\widetilde{O}(m^k)\)-time algorithm is trivial for even vertex paths and cycles in general graphs. By assuming that the host is bipartite, we slighly improve on this running-time, and only for \(m=\Theta(n^{1+\epsilon})\), \(0\le\epsilon<1\) for cycles. We

also note that Hoàng, Kaminski, Sawada and Sritharan \[6\] gave a \(\widetilde{O}(nm^{k-1})\)- time algorithm for finding _P_2_k_ in _general graphs_ (They do not give algorithms for finding induced cycles). ## 2 Preliminaries We begin by defining standard notions of containment in graph theory. **Definition 1 (Subgraph).** _Let H_=(_VH,EH_) _and G_=(_VG,EG_) _be graphs. We say that G is a_ subgraph _of H, denoted by_ \(G\subseteq H\)_, if_ \(V_G\subseteq V_H\text{\textit{and}}E_G\subseteq\{\{u,v\}\in E_H:u,v\in V_G\}.\) **Definition 2 (Induced Subgraph).** _Let G_=(_V,E_) _be a graph and let_ \(T\subseteq V\)_. The induced subgraph of G on T, denoted G_\[_T_\]_, is the graph whose vertex set is T and whose edge set consists of all edges of G with both endpoints in T._ **Definition 3 (Minor).** _Let H and G be graphs. We say that G is a_ minor _of H (denoted_ \(G\unknown H\)_) if G can be obtained from H by a finite sequence of the operations like vertex deletions, edge deletions and edge contractions._ **Definition 4 (Edge Contraction).** _Let H_=(_VH,EH_) _be a graph and let_ \(e=\{u,v\}\in E_H\)_. The graph obtained by_ contracting _e, denoted by H/e, is defined as follows._ _Let_ \(E'=\{\ell\in E_H:u\in\ell\text{\textit{or}}v\in\ell\}\) _be the set of edges incident to u or v, and let_ \(E''=\big\{\{u',w\}:w\in(N_H(u)\cup N_H(v))\backslash\{u,v\}\big\}.\) _where_ \(H/e=(V_{H/e},E_{H/e})\)
\(V_{H/e}=(V_H\backslash\{u,v\})\cup\{u'\}\)
\(E_{H/e}=(E_H\backslash E')\cup E''\) . _Here,_ \(u'\) _is a new vertex representing the contraction of u and v._ We now define tree decompositions and path decompositions, which are useful for designing dynamic programming algorithms on graphs. **Definition 5 (Tree Decomposition).** _A_ tree decomposition _of a graph G_=(_V,E_) _is a pair_ \((\mathcal{T},\{X_t\}_{t\in V(\mathcal{T})})\) _where_ T _is a tree and each node t is assigned a subset_ \(X_t\subseteq V\)_, called a bag, such that: (1)_ \(\bigcup_{t\in V(\mathcal{T})}X_t=V\)_, (2) for every edge_ \(\{u,v\}\in E\)_, there exists t with_ \(\{u,v\}\subseteq X_t\)_, and (3) for every vertex_ \(v\in V\)_, the set_ \(\{t|v\in X_t\}\) _induces a connected subtree of_ T _. The width of a tree decomposition is_ max_t|Xt_|-1_. The treewidth of G, denoted_ tw(_G), is the minimum width over all tree decompositions of G._

**Definition 6 (Path Decomposition).** _A path decomposition is a tree decomposition in which the underlying tree_ T _is a path. The pathwidth of G, denoted_ pw(_G), is the minimum width over all path decompositions of G._

Finally, we define arithmetic circuits.

**Definition 7 (Arithmetic Circuit).** _An arithmetic circuit over a ring R is a directed acyclic graph whose nodes are of three types: (1) input nodes labeled by variables or constants from R, (2) addition gates labeled_ +_, (3) multiplication gates labeled_ \(\times\).

_Each gate computes a polynomial over R in the natural way. The output gate computes the polynomial defined by the circuit._

_The_ size of a circuit _is the number of gates, and the_ depth _is the length of the longest directed path from an input node to the output gate._

**Definition 8 (Induced Subgraph Polynomial).** _For a k-vertex pattern G and a host H, we define the_ induced subgraph polynomial _as_<tbc>

\(Ind_{G,H}\big((y_v)_{v\in V(H)}\big)=\sum_{S\subseteq V(H)|S|=kH[S]\cong G}\prod_{v\in S}y_v.\)

<tbc>**Definition 9 (Subgraph Polynomial).** _For a k-vertex pattern G and a host H, we define the_ subgraph polynomial _as_

\(Sub_{G,H}\big((y_v)_{v\in V(H)}\big)=\sum_{S\subseteq V(H)|S|=kH[S]\supseteq G}\alpha_S\prod_{v\in S}y_v,\)

_where_ \(H[S]\supseteq G\) _means that H_\[_S_\] _contains a subgraph isomorphic to G, and_ \(\alpha_S\) _denotes the number of such subgraphs in H_\[_S_\].

**Definition 10 (Homomorphism Polynomial).** _For a k-vertex pattern G and a host H, we define the_ homomorphism polynomial _as_<tbc>

\(Hom_{G,H}\big((y_v)_{v\in V(H)}\big)=\sum_\phi\prod_{v\in V(G)}y_{\phi(v)},\)

<tbc>_where_ \(\phi\) _ranges over all homomorphisms from G to H. A_ homomorphism _is a map_ \(\phi:V(G)\rightarrow V(H)\) _such that_

\(\{u,v\}\in E(G)\Longrightarrow\{\phi(u),\phi(v)\}\in E(H).\)

### 3 Small Circuits for Homomorphism Polynomials from Tree Decompositions

We begin by defining a new notion of width for tree decompositions.

<tbc>**Definition 11.** _A tree decomposition T of G has_ width (_p,q_) _if for each bag B of T, there exist vertices_ \(u_1,\dots,u_i\in B\) _with_ \(i\le p\) _and edges_ \(e_1,\dots,e_j\in E(G[B])\) _with_ \(j\le q\) _such that_

\(E\big(G[B]\backslash\{u_1,\dots,u_i\}\big)=\{e_1,\dots,e_j\},\)

_and moreover every vertex of B_\\{_u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>i</sub>_} _is an endpoint of some_ \(e_\ell\), \(\ell\le j\).

_We say that the vertices u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>i</sub> and edges e_<sub>1</sub>_,...,e<sub>j</sub> is a_ (_p,q_)-witness _of the bag B._

The same edge could occur in multiple bags in a tree decomposition. We have to ensure that an edge occuring in the image of a homomorphism is only multiplied in once in the term corresponding to the homomorphism. We define a notion of _local vertex_ for this purpose.

**Definition 12.** _Let T be a tree decomposition of G. Fix a function_ \(f:V(G)\rightarrow V(T)\) _assigning each vertex_ \(v\in V(G)\) _to some bag f(v_) _(such a bag exists by the definition of tree decomposition). We say v is_ local _to bag B if f(v_)=_B, and write_

\(V_B=\{v\in V(G):f(v)=B\}.\)

Note that since _f_ is a function, each vertex of _G_ is local to exactly one bag in the tree decomposition.

We now prove that we can efficiently construct circuits for homomorphism polynomials from (_p,q_)-width tree decompositions. Our proof is a refinement of the dynamic programming algorithm by Díaz, Serna, and Thilikos \[4\].

**Theorem 1.** _Let G be a k-vertex pattern graph having a tree decomposition T of_ (_p,q)-width, and let H be a host graph with n vertices and m edges. Then an arithmetic circuit of size O(n<sup>p</sup>m<sup>q</sup>_) _computing Hom<sub>G,H</sub> can be constructed in time_ \(\widetilde{O}(n^pm^q)\).

_Proof._ We describe the construction of the arithmetic circuit for Hom<sub>_G,H_</sub>.

Let _T_ be a tree decomposition of _G_ of (_p,q_)-width, rooted at the bag _R_. For any bag _B_ in _T_, let _T<sub>B</sub>_ denote the subtree of _T_ rooted at _B_, and define

\(G_B=G[V'],\text{where}V'=\bigcup_{B^\prime\in V(T_B)}B'\)

.

The circuit will have two kinds of gates, denoted by \(g_{B,\phi}\) and \(h_{B,\phi}\), where _B_ is a bag in _T_ and \(\phi\) is some partial homomorphism from _G_ to _H_ defined on a subgraph of _G_ to be specified later.

We define \(g_{B,\phi}\) so that the polynomial computed at \(g_{B,\phi}\) is:

\(g_{B,\phi}=\sum_{\phi^\prime:G_B\rightarrow H\phi^\prime\sim\phi}\prod_{v\in V(G_B)v\text{is local to some bag in}T_B}y_{\phi^\prime(v)}\) (1)

Here, \(\phi\) is any homomorphism from _G_\[_B_\] to _H_. We say that \(\phi'\) is _compatible_ with \(\phi\), denoted by \(\phi'\sim\phi\), iff

\(\phi'(v)=\phi(v)\text{for every}v\text{where}\phi(v)\text{and}\phi'(v)\text{are defined.}\)

Let _B_ be any non-root bag with a parent \(B'\). We add gates \(h_{B,\phi}\), where \(\phi\) is a homomorphism from \(G[B\cap B']\) to _H_. These gates will compute the following polynomial:

\(h_{B,\phi}=\sum_{\phi^\prime:G[B]\mapsto H\phi^\prime\sim\phi} g_{B,\phi^\prime}.\) (2)

We now construct the circuit by traversing the tree decomposition _T_ in a bottom-up fashion.

#### Leaf bags:

Suppose that _B_ is a leaf of _T_. Then _G<sub>B</sub>=G_\[_B_\]. There are no child bags, and hence all vertices of _G<sub>B</sub>_ that are local to _B_ can be introduced directly. For every \(\phi:G[B]\mapsto G\), we create the product gate

\(g_{B,\phi}=\prod_{v\in V(G[B])v\text{is local to}B}y_{\phi(v)}.\)

Note that we can enumerate all such \(\phi\) in _O(n<sup>p</sup>m<sup>q</sup>_) time by enumerating all possible images of the (_p,q_)-witness _u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>i</sub>_ and _e_<sub>1</sub>_,...,e<sub>j</sub>_ of the bag _B_ where \(i\le p\) and \(j\le q\). This can be done by enumerating all elements of \(V(H)^i\times E(H)^j\).

#### Non-leaf bags:

Now suppose that _B_ is a non-leaf bag with children _B_<sub>1</sub>_,...,B<sub>r</sub>_. For every homomorphism \(\phi:G[B]\mapsto H\), we add the following gate:

\(g_{B,\phi}=\left(\prod_{i=1}^rh_{B_i,\phi|_{B\cap B_i}}\right)\cdot\left(\prod_{v\in V(G[B])v\text{is local to}B}y_{\phi(v)}\right).\) (3)

#### The gates \(h_{B,\phi}\):

The gates \(h_{B,\phi}\) can be constructed as follows: When we construct a gate \(g_{B,\phi^\prime}\) for some \(\phi':G[B]\mapsto H\), we compute \(\phi\sim\phi'\) such that \(\phi:G[B\cap B']\mapsto H\) and then add the gate \(g_{B,\phi^\prime}\) as an input to the +-gate \(h_{B,\phi}\).

#### The output gate:

Finally, the output gate of our circuit is a +-gate that adds all \(g_{R,\phi}\), where _R_ is the root bag in _T_.

#### Correctness:

We prove that the gates \(g_{B,\phi}\) compute the polynomial in Equation 1 using induction. Note that _G<sub>R</sub>=G_ and therefore our output gate will correctly compute Hom<sub>_G,H_</sub> given that all \(g_{B,\phi}\) and \(h_{B,\phi}\) are as claimed.

In the base case, _B_ is a leaf bag and the construction directly computes the required polynomial.

<tbc>In the inductive case, _B_ is a non-leaf bag with children _B_<sub>1</sub>_,...,B<sub>r</sub>_. Let \(\phi:G_B\mapsto H\). First, we show that the the monomial corresponding to \(\phi\) in Equation 1 is generated by the gate \(g_{B,\phi^\prime}\) as in Equation 3 where \(\phi':G[B]\mapsto H\) is the unique homomorphism such that \(\phi'\sim\phi\). Similarly, let \(\phi_i:G_{B_i}\mapsto H\) be the unique homomorphisms such that \(\phi_i\sim\phi\) for \(1\le i\le r\). Let \(\phi'_i:G[B\cap B_i]\mapsto H\) be the unique homomorphisms such that \(\phi'_i\sim\phi_i\) for \(1\le i\le r\). By the induction hypothesis, \(h_{B_i,\phi_i^\prime}\) will contain the monomial corresponding to \(\phi_i\) (notice that \(\phi|_{B\cap B_i}=\phi'_i\)). For this choice of \(\phi'_i\) for all \(1\le i\le r\), the first factor in the product in Equation 3 will include all \(y_{\phi(v)}\) where _v_ is local to some bag in _T<sub>B</sub>_ that is not _B_. The second factor will include all \(y_{\phi^\prime(v)(=\phi(v))}\) for _v_ that is local to _B_. Therefore the monomial corresponding to \(\phi'=\phi\) in the summation of Equation 1 is generated at the gate Equation 3. Observe that since the decomposition of \(\phi\) into \(\phi'\) and \(\phi_i\) for \(1\le i\le r\) in the above argument is unique, the monomial corresponding to \(\phi\) is also generated exactly once.

We now show that all monomials generated by the gate \(g_{B,\phi^\prime}\) as in Equation 3 correspond to valid homomorphisms. Observe that inductively the contribution of the first factor in all monomials generated correspond to valid homomorphisms \(\phi_i:G_{B_i}\mapsto H\). By the connectivity property of tree decompositions, any vertex _v_ appearing in both _G<sub>B<sub>i</sub></sub>_ and _G<sub>B<sub>j</sub></sub>_ for \(i\neq j\) must also appear in _B_. Therefore, \(\phi_i(v)=\phi_j(v)=\phi'(v)\) ensuring that any monomial produced at this gate corresponds to a valid homomorphism.

The gates \(h_{B,\phi}\) are correct because we compute them in exactly the same way we defined them in Equation 2.

### Time complexity of the construction:

We now prove that the running-time of the construction algorithm is \(\widetilde{O}(n^pm^q)\). Since the pattern graph _G_ is fixed, there are at most _O(n<sup>p</sup>m<sup>q</sup>_) pairs \((B,\phi)\) where \(\phi:G[B]\mapsto H\). The gates \(g_{B,\phi}\) are constructed by simply iterating over all such pairs and the amount of work done per gate is logarithmic in the size of the input. This is because give \((B,\phi)\), we can compute the indices of the _h_ gates in constant-time and then look up \(h_{B_i,\phi|_{B\cap B_i}}\) in _O_(log_n_)-time. Notice that the size of the circuit is _O(n<sup>p</sup>m<sup>q</sup>_) as each wire in the circuit is incident on some \(g_{B,\phi}\) which has only constant number of inputs and feeds its output to exactly one _h_ gate.

## 4 Using Homomorphisms for Finding Induced Subgraphs

Our algorithms are generalizations of algorithms for detecting small induced patterns given by Bläser, Komarath, and Sreenivasaiah \[1\] and Komarath, Kumar, Mishra, and Sethia \[7\]. For completeness, we describe the general method here.

Using inclusion-exclusion, the induced subgraph polynomial (Definition 8) can be expressed in terms of subgraph polynomials (Definition 9) as

\(\mathrm{Ind}_{G,H}=\sum_{G^\prime\supseteq G}(-1)^{|E(G^\prime)|-|E(G)|}\alpha_{G,G^\prime}\mathrm{Sub}_{G^\prime,H},\)

where \(\alpha_{G,G^\prime}\) denotes the number of subgraphs of \(G'\) that are isomorphic to _G_.

<tbc>_Example 1._ Let _H_ be the graph _K_<sub>3</sub>+_e_ which is a triangle on vertices 1,2, and 3 and an edge {3,4}. Then, we have Ind<sub>_P_<sub>3</sub>_,H_</sub>=_y_<sub>1</sub>_y_<sub>3</sub>_y_<sub>4</sub>+_y_<sub>2</sub>_y_<sub>3</sub>_y_<sub>4</sub>, Sub<sub>_P_<sub>3</sub>_,H_</sub>=3_y_<sub>1</sub>_y_<sub>2</sub>_y_<sub>3</sub>+_y_<sub>1</sub>_y_<sub>3</sub>_y_<sub>4</sub>+_y_<sub>2</sub>_y_<sub>3</sub>_y_<sub>4</sub>, and Sub<sub>_K_<sub>3</sub>_,H_</sub>=_y_<sub>1</sub>_y_<sub>2</sub>_y_<sub>3</sub>. By the above inclusion- exclusion formula, we have Ind<sub>_P_<sub>3</sub>_,H_</sub>=Sub<sub>_P_<sub>3</sub>_,H_</sub>-3Sub<sub>_K_<sub>3</sub>_,H_</sub>.

Given an _H_, the problem of detecting whether there is an induced _G_ in _H_ is the same as checking whether the polynomial Ind<sub>_G,H_</sub> is not the identity (zero) polynomial. Since the coefficients of all monomials are either 0 or 1 in Ind<sub>_G,H_</sub>, this is equivalent to testing whether it is non-zero modulo _p_ for any prime _p_. In the above example, we can take _p_=3 and then checking whether \(\mathrm{Ind}_{P_3,H}\neq 0\) is equivalent to checking \(\mathrm{Sub}_{P_3,H}\neq 0\). That is, taking modulo 3 eliminated the Sub<sub>_K_<sub>3</sub>_,H_</sub>. It remains to compute Sub<sub>_P_<sub>3</sub>_,H_</sub> efficiently given _H_. However, we don’t know how to do this. Instead, we compute a polynomial where the multilinear monomials correspond to the monomials of Sub<sub>_P_<sub>3</sub>_,H_</sub> and then test whether this new polynomial has a multilinear monomial.

The multilinear monomials of Hom<sub>_P_<sub>3</sub>_,H_</sub> are in 2-to-1 correspondence with the monomials of Sub<sub>_P_<sub>3</sub>_,H_</sub>. This is because _P_<sub>3</sub> has two automorphisms. Therefore, we have now reduced the problem to that of checking whether Hom<sub>_P_<sub>3</sub>_,H_</sub> has a multilinear monomial modulo 3. There is a linear-time algorithm to check whether the polynomial has a multilinear monomial modulo _p_ given a circuit computing it for any _p_ given by Koutis and Williams \[8\]. Moreover, the polynomial Hom<sub>_P_<sub>3</sub>_,H_</sub> can be computed in _O(n+m_)-time as \(\sum_{v\in V(H)}y_v(\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E(H)}y_u)^2\). Therefore, we have a _O(n+m_)-time algorithm for detecting induced _P_<sub>3</sub>.

For the pattern _P_<sub>4</sub>, the above method is not as straightforward as we have to do arithmetic modulo 2 to obtain Ind<sub>_P_<sub>4</sub>_,H_</sub>=Sub<sub>_P_<sub>4</sub>_,H_</sub>. But _P_<sub>4</sub> also has two automorphisms. Therefore, modulo 2 arithmetic will eliminate all multilinear monomials from Hom<sub>_P_<sub>4</sub>_,H_</sub>. We can circumvent this problem by ensuring that only the multilinear monomials corresponding to _P_<sub>4</sub>-homomorphisms where \(\phi(2)<\phi(3)\) survive. We call this condition an _automorphism avoiding condition_. Now, the multilinear monomials of that polynomial will be the same as that of Sub<sub>_P_<sub>4</sub>_,H_</sub>. We sketch the part of the dynamic programming algorithm based on a tree decomposition of _P_<sub>4</sub> to show how this is ensured. Consider _P_<sub>4</sub> labeled as 1--2--3--4 and the tree decomposition _B_<sub>1</sub>--_B_<sub>2</sub>--_B_<sub>3</sub> where _B_<sub>1</sub>={1,2}, _B_<sub>2</sub>={2,3} and _B_<sub>3</sub>={3,4}. For each bag _B<sub>i</sub>_, the algorithm iterates over elements of _V(H_)<sup>|_B<sub>i</sub>_|</sup> and checks whether we can map the vertices in _B<sub>i</sub>_ to the elements in this tuple. So when we iterate over _V(H_)<sup>2</sup> for the bag _B_<sub>2</sub> and we consider the element (_u,v_), we will check that \(\{u,v\}\in E(H)\) and that _u\<v_ (This is the check \(\phi(2)<\phi(3)\)). Therefore for any _P_<sub>4</sub>-subgraph where {_u,v_} is the middle edge, we only account for it once in the final polynomial.

We have already seen in Section 3 how to use (_p,q_)-width tree decompositions to produce circuits of size _O(n<sup>p</sup>m<sup>q</sup>_) for homomorphism polynomials. In the coming sections, we show that these improved constructions along with the above idea can be used to derive faster algorithms for many patterns.

## 5 Faster Algorithms for Small Patterns

For detecting induced isomorphisms, simply constructing the homomorphism polynomial using Theorem 1 is not sufficient. As described in Section 4, we also have to show existence of decompositions that avoids automorphisms. In this section, we do that for many small pattern graphs. Note that since (_p,q_)- width tree decompositions are tree decompositions \(p+2q\ge w+1\) where _w_ is the treewidth. So for a non-tree, five vertex pattern, the best we can hope for is _p_=1_,q_=1. ### 6 Induced Paths and Cycles in Bipartite Graphs

In this section, we consider a simple extension of the dynamic programming algorithms given by Díaz, Serna and Thilikos \[4\] and Komarath, Kumar, Mishra and Sethia \[7\] that constructs polynomials different from the homomorphism polynomial. Suppose a bag _B_ in the tree decomposition of the pattern graph _G_ that we use in the dynamic programming algorithm contains vertices _u_ and _v_ such that \(\{u,v\}\unknown\in E(H)\) for the input graph _H_. Then, we can remove monomials that correspond to any homomorphism \(\phi\) from _G_ to _H_ where \(\{\phi(u),\phi(v)\}\in E(H)\) while building the arithmetic circuit for Hom<sub>_G,H_</sub>. We use this idea to obtain the following improved algorithms for detecting induced even length paths and cycles in bipartite graphs.

**Theorem 5.** _Given an m-edge bipartite host graph H as input, we can detect whether H has an induced P_<sub>2_k_</sub> _in_ \(\widetilde{O}(m^{k-1})\)_-time._

_Proof._ We consider the following (0_,k_-1)-width path decomposition of _P_<sub>2_k_</sub>: _B_<sub>1</sub>--_B_<sub>2</sub>--_B_<sub>3</sub> where _B_<sub>1</sub>={1_,...,_2_k_-2}, _B_<sub>2</sub>={2_,...,_2_k_-1}, and _B_<sub>3</sub>={3_,...,_2_k_}. We add conditions to check that the graph induced on images of {1_,...,_2_k_-2} does not have any edges other than that in the labeled _P_<sub>2_k_</sub> using the bag _B_<sub>1</sub>. Similar checks can be done for the bags _B_<sub>2</sub> and _B_<sub>3</sub> as well. Therefore, the only edges other than the ones in labeled _P_<sub>2_k_</sub> will be _e_<sub>1</sub>={1,2_k_}, _e_<sub>2</sub>={1,2_k_-1}, _e_<sub>3</sub>={2,2_k_}. Among these _e_<sub>2</sub> and _e_<sub>3</sub> cannot exist if {1_,...,_2_k_} is a path as that would form an odd cycle in _H_, which is not possible in a bipartite graph _H_. Therefore, the only supergraph of _P_<sub>2_k_</sub> appearing as monomials would be _C_<sub>2_k_</sub>. But a _C_<sub>2_k_</sub> contains a _P_<sub>2_k_</sub> an even number of times. So evaluation over rings of characteristic two will eliminate it. In addition, we use the condition that \(\phi(k)<\phi(k+1)\) to remove one of the automorphisms of _P_<sub>2_k_</sub> from the polynomial. Therefore, the multilinear monomials of the constructed polynomial is in one-to- one correspondence with the monomials of Ind<sub>_P_<sub>2_k_</sub>_,H_</sub> (and not Sub<sub>_P_<sub>2_k_</sub>_,H_</sub>). Since this arithmetic circuit can be constructed and evaluated in \(\widetilde{O}(m^{k-1})\)-time, the theorem follows.

**Theorem 6.** _Given an n-vertex, m-edge bipartite host graph H as input, we can detect whether H has an induced C_<sub>2_k_</sub> _in_ \(\widetilde{O}(nm^{k-1})\)_-time._

_Proof._ We consider the following (1_,k_-1)-width path decomposition for _C_<sub>2_k_</sub>: _B_<sub>1</sub>--_B_<sub>2</sub> where _B_<sub>1</sub>={1_,...,_2_k_-1} and _B_<sub>2</sub>={1,3_,...,_2_k_}. Then, we add the check that in _B_<sub>1</sub> and _B_<sub>2</sub> edges other than the ones in the labeled _C_<sub>2_k_</sub> are absent. The only remaining edge that could occur is {2,2_k_}. But this edge in _C_<sub>2_k_</sub> would lead to an odd cycle, which is not possible in a bipartite _H_. We also add the check \(\phi(1)<\phi(i)\) for all \(i\neq 1\). Therefore, only two automorphisms of _C_<sub>2_k_</sub> will survive. The multilinear part of the resulting polynomial is exactly 2Ind<sub>_C_<sub>2_k_</sub>_,H_</sub>. To check that Ind<sub>_C_<sub>2_k_</sub>_,H_</sub> is non-zero, we can simply check whether the computed polynomial has a non-zero multilinear monomial modulo 3.

### A An example finding 4-paths in Bull graph B

For the homomorphism polynomial, \(Hom_{P_4,\mathcal{B}}((y_v)_{v\in V(\mathcal{B})})\), consider variables \(y_v\in R\), where _R_ is a commutative ring with characteristic char(_R_)=2, and _y_<sup>2</sup>=0 for all \(y\in R\). The automorphism group of _P_<sub>4</sub> has two elements, the identity and the reversal 1-2-3-4 \(\leftrightarrow\) 4-3-2-1. Therefore, each homomorphism from _P_<sub>4</sub> to B contributes a coefficient of 2 to the corresponding monomial in the homomorphism polynomial. Since we are working over a ring of characteristic 2, all coefficients are even and hence vanish identically over _R_. The even number of

automorphisms of _P_<sub>4</sub> can be eliminated by imposing the condition \(\phi(2)<\phi(3)\) on the homomorphisms \(\phi:V(P_4)\mapsto V(\mathcal{B})\). The four types of monomials present in the homomorphism polynomial are as follows:

#### Homomorphisms onto a single edge.

If all three edges of _P_<sub>4</sub> (i.e., 1-2, 2-3, 3-4) map onto the same edge \((i,j)\in E(\mathcal{B})\), the contribution is

\(\sum_{(i,j)\in E(\mathcal{B})}2y_i^2y_j^2.\)

Since this term carries a square factor \(y_i^2\), it vanishes identically over _R_.

#### Homomorphisms onto a 2-edge walk.

If the image of _P_<sub>4</sub> revisits a vertex, for example, 1-2-3-4 \(\mapsto\) _a-b-c-a_, the resulting monomial still contains a repeated (squared) variable, and hence again vanishes due to the property of the ring R.

#### Homomorphisms where P_<sub>4</sub> _embeds as a subgraph._

When the image of _P_<sub>4</sub> is an actual (injective) subgraph of B, no variable is repeated, and the resulting monomial is multilinear, these are the terms in the homomorphism polynomial which can contribute to induced subgraph counting.

For example, take 1-2-3-4 \(\mapsto\) _a-b-e-d_. The automorphism group of _P_<sub>4</sub> (reversal, 1-2-3-4 \(\leftrightarrow\) 4-3-2-1) maps this to the same image, contributing the term _y<sub>a</sub>y<sub>b</sub>y<sub>e</sub>y<sub>d</sub>_ with coefficient 2. Because B contains the extra edge _b-e_, there is a second homomorphism, 1-2-3-4 \(\mapsto\) _b-a-e-d_, which (together with its own reversal) contributes the same monomial _y<sub>a</sub>y<sub>b</sub>y<sub>e</sub>y<sub>d</sub>_ with coefficient 2 as well. ### Homomorphisms where P<sub>4</sub> embeds as an induced subgraph.

Here the image _P_<sub>4</sub> is an _induced_ copy in B; with no variable repeated and no extra edge between the vertices in the host graph, resulting in a multilinear monomial with co-efficient 2 (the path and its reversal).

For example, take 1-2-3-4 \(\mapsto\) _c-b-e-d_. The automorphism group of _P_<sub>4</sub> consists of the identity and the reversal 1-2-3-4 \(\leftrightarrow\) 4-3-2-1; the reversal sends this mapping to 1-2-3-4 \(\mapsto\) _d-e-b-c_, which is the same walk traversed backward and hence produces the identical monomial _y<sub>c</sub>y<sub>b</sub>y<sub>e</sub>y<sub>d</sub>_. So when we impose the conditions \((\phi(2)<\phi(3))\) to avoid automorphisms, the coefficient becomes odd for all induced copies.

Hence only the multilinear terms of the homomorphism polynomial contributing to the _induced_ subgraph survives, as the terms in the first 3 cases vanish. The terms in the third case vanishes due to even coefficients, since the imposed condition doesn’t stop it from counting the extra _P_<sub>4</sub> due to the extra edge.

## Verification procedure.

The function `verify_decomposition` checks whether a given sequence of bags is valid for parameters _p_ and _q_. Each bag must be (_p,q_)- spannable: after removing _p_ vertices, the remaining vertices are covered by the endpoints of _q_ edges. This is verified by enumerating all choices of removed vertices and testing edge coverage in the induced subgraph.

The procedure also checks that every comparability condition _i\<j_ is witnessed by some bag, and that the number of graph automorphisms preserving all such conditions is odd. Any violation causes the verification to fail with an explicit error.
